name: Tony Strickland
title: California State Senator, Vice Chair of the Senate Labor, Public Employment and Retirement Committee and the Senate Transportation Committee
district: California State Senate District 36 (Huntington Beach and surrounding coastal Orange County)
years_of_service: March 11, 2025–present in his current Senate term (won a special election outright on February 25, 2025 with 51.3% of the vote; current term ends December 7, 2026). This is Strickland's second stint in the State Senate; he also served December 1, 2008–December 3, 2012, representing the former District 19. (Source: Ballotpedia, Tony Strickland.)
background: Strickland was born at Fort Ord, California in 1970 while his father was stationed there; his family moved to Ventura County in 1973. He earned a B.A. in political science from Whittier College, where he received the Leadership and Service Award and was named a Nixon Scholar. From 1996 to 1997 he worked on the staff of then-Assemblyman Tom McClintock. (Source: Wikipedia, Tony Strickland — used here because Ballotpedia's own biography section for Strickland is a single sentence and does not cover his early life; this is an explicit fallback to Wikipedia for that material.)

Strickland was first elected to the California State Assembly in 1998, representing the 37th district, winning a three-way race with 49% of the vote. He was re-elected in 2000 with 51% and in 2002 with 63.1%, serving until November 30, 2004. In December 1999, the California Secretary of State sued Strickland for failing to timely report $116,140 in late campaign contributions, a violation of the state's Political Reform Act; he was fined $6,000. (Sources: Ballotpedia, Tony Strickland; Wikipedia, Tony Strickland, for the 1999 FPPC/Secretary of State matter, which Ballotpedia's page does not mention.)

In 2006 and again in 2010, Strickland ran for California State Controller. He won both Republican primaries (40.7% in 2006, 60.1% in 2010) but lost both general elections to Democrat John Chiang (50.7%–40.2% in 2006; 55%–36% in 2010). In April 2010, the state Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC) fined him $3,000 for sending mass mailings that lacked the required committee-name disclosure on the exterior. In May 2016, Strickland agreed to pay $40,000 to settle an FPPC investigation that found he had laundered campaign donations during his 2010 controller run by routing contributions through county Republican party committees to evade individual contribution limits; he accepted responsibility for eight violations. (Source: Wikipedia, Tony Strickland; these FPPC matters are not covered on Ballotpedia's page.)

Strickland was elected to the State Senate in 2008, representing the 19th district, in an extremely close race against Democrat Hannah-Beth Jackson: 207,976 votes to 207,119, a margin of 857 votes. He served one term, through December 3, 2012, sitting on committees including Health (Vice Chair) and Environmental Quality (Vice Chair). Rather than seek re-election against Sen. Fran Pavley after redistricting combined portions of their districts in 2012, Strickland instead ran for the U.S. House seat in California's 26th Congressional District; he advanced from the primary but lost the general election to Democrat Julia Brownley, 52.7%–47.3%. In 2014 he ran again for Congress, in the newly drawn 25th District, advancing from the top-two primary but losing the general election to fellow Republican Steve Knight, 53.3%–46.7%; his 2014 campaign was endorsed by retiring Rep. Buck McKeon, Mitt Romney, and Paul Ryan. In October 2015 he formed and served as president and CEO of Strong America, a federal super PAC. (Source: Ballotpedia, Tony Strickland; Wikipedia, Tony Strickland, for the Strong America super PAC, which Ballotpedia's page does not mention.)

Strickland served on the Huntington Beach City Council from December 2022 to March 2025 and as Mayor of Huntington Beach from December 2022 to December 2023. As mayor and councilmember he was a vocal opponent of state housing mandates, backing the city's move to stop accepting accessory dwelling unit applications; California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued Huntington Beach over the move, alleging violations of the state's SB 9 (HOME Act) accessory-dwelling-unit law, and a federal judge denied the city's request for a temporary restraining order against the state. Strickland has argued Huntington Beach is "95% built out" and has opposed measures he says would change the character of the city. Note: Strickland owns a home in Moorpark, California, but available sources (Wikipedia, Ballotpedia) do not show he ever held elected office in Moorpark — he was never a Moorpark City Council member or mayor; his only municipal office was in Huntington Beach. (Source: Wikipedia, Tony Strickland.)

Strickland won a February 25, 2025 special primary election outright, with 51.3% of the vote against three opponents, to fill the vacant State Senate District 36 seat, returning to the Senate after a 12-year absence. He is running for a full term in the November 3, 2026 general election against Democrat Chris Duncan, having advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary with 55.6% of the vote to Duncan's 44.4%. In July 2025, while already back in the Senate, he co-filed the Proposition 39 voter-ID and citizenship-verification initiative with Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and Donald DiCostanzo; that measure's substance, funding, and campaign are covered in content/measures/ca-prop-39-2026.json and are not duplicated here. (Source: Ballotpedia, Tony Strickland.)

voting_record_highlights: SB 885 (2025–2026), the Restoring Accountability Act, which would require legislative approval for major state regulatory proposals exceeding $50 million in fiscal impact: Strickland is the lead author, with Sens. Jones, Niello, Ochoa Bogh, and Seyarto as coauthors. The Senate policy committee voted 4–1 on April 14, 2026 to recommend passage with re-referral to Appropriations, but the bill status record shows it "failed passage in committee" at that hearing, with reconsideration granted. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill status for SB 885.)

SB 926 (2025–2026), appropriating $280 million from the General Fund for Fiscal Year 2026–27 for Proposition 36 behavioral-health and drug-treatment implementation: Strickland is the lead author. The Senate Appropriations Committee voted 7–0 (Ayes 7, Noes 0) to pass the bill on May 11, 2026, but it was placed on the Appropriations suspense file and held under submission after a May 14, 2026 hearing; that is the last status this profile could confirm. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill status for SB 926.)

SB 1015 (2025–2026), the Protecting Our Children from Online Extortion Act, creating a new criminal offense for predators who coerce minors into exploiting other minors: Strickland is the sole named author. The Assembly Public Safety Committee voted 9–0 to pass the bill as amended on June 23, 2026, but after re-referral to Assembly Appropriations the bill was held in committee and under submission as of August 13, 2026, the last status this profile could confirm. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill status for SB 1015.)
attendance: No individually published floor-attendance or voting-participation record for Senator Strickland was found. As with other California State Senate members, the Senate does not publish a per-member attendance scorecard; the only public records are bill-by-bill roll-call votes at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which is what the voting-record entries above are drawn from. Ballotpedia's page for Strickland notes it is "in the process" of compiling third-party legislative scorecards for him but does not itself publish an attendance metric.
